Samuel Willard
sam'yōo-êl wil'êrd
n. (Samuel Willard, 1640–1707, minister of Boston's Old South Church, acting President of Harvard, author of A Compleat Body of Divinity)
English Willard, Germanic, bold in will; Samuel, from Hebrew Shemu'el, heard of God.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Samuel Willard preached through the Westminster Shorter Catechism, question by question, on Tuesday lectures for nineteen years. The sermons were gathered after his death into A Compleat Body of Divinity, published in 1726 and the largest book printed in colonial America: a full Reformed systematic theology produced not in a university but in a parish, delivered to shopkeepers and sailors. He was also the minister who sheltered an accused woman from the Salem proceedings and was himself cried out upon for it, and he served as acting President of Harvard from 1701. Col 1:28 describes exactly what he was doing, preaching Christ and “warning every man, and teaching every man in all wisdom.” 2Ti 4:2 commanded the persistence. Act 20:27 names the completeness he aimed at, not shunning to declare all the counsel of God — which in his case took nineteen years of Tuesdays.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a catechism as a form of instruction by means of questions and answers; and divinity, as the science of divine things; theology.

expand to see more

CAT'ECHISM, n. A form of instruction by means of questions and answers, particularly in the principles of religion.

DIVIN'ITY, n. The science of divine things; the science which unfolds the character of God, his laws and moral government.

LEC'TURE, n. A discourse read or pronounced on any subject; a formal or methodical discourse.

2Ti 4:2 — "Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine."

Act 20:27 — "For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God."

Modern Corruption

Nineteen years of Tuesday lectures on the Shorter Catechism produced the largest book printed in colonial America.

expand to see more

The achievement is a rebuke to the assumption that systematic theology belongs to academies. Willard's hearers were a Boston congregation, and he gave them the doctrine of God, the decrees, the covenants, the person and work of Christ, the application of redemption and the last things, in order, at the pace of a sermon a week. Col 1:28 sets the goal of such labour as presenting every man perfect in Christ Jesus, and the teaching is given to every man, not to the capable few.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live failure is the assumption that congregations cannot bear doctrine and must be fed anecdote. 2Ti 4:2 pairs preaching the word with longsuffering and doctrine in a single clause, and the longsuffering is required because the doctrine takes time. Act 20:27 makes completeness a ministerial duty; a pulpit that never reaches the hard chapters has shunned part of the counsel of God.

Usage

"“Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2) — nineteen years of it."

"“all the counsel of God” (Act 20:27) — the completeness he aimed at."
